title: Ballast Weather
passage:
Jointed track left a winter gap at every fishplate for summer to close; welded rail has no such luxury. It has nowhere to put the extra millimetres, so what would have been movement becomes force, and whether the force goes anywhere is settled by stone: the ballast packed between the sleepers and, above all, the shoulder heaped beyond their ends. A tamping machine lifts the track and packs new stone underneath, and for eight weeks afterwards that stone is loose. Twenty-seven degrees is the stress-free temperature in Isak Vessholm's district; it tells him how hard a July afternoon will push against the rail, and nothing about what is resisting it. His log runs to 39 buckles – track shoved sideways out of line – across 19 summers, and two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work. The hottest week on record produced none. Gangs are sent wherever somebody has reported something, Vessholm says, so the quieter miles go uncounted.
– Esme Quillenby

questions.prompt: What are we told about the buckles in Vessholm's log?

options.text: That a gang usually turned up to work the ballast within weeks of one appearing.
That two thirds of them came soon after a tamping machine had been through.
That they all fell in the eight weeks following a tamping machine's visit.
That most of them fell in the hottest weeks the district has on record.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail: the key paraphrases the log's own tally. The passage states that Vessholm's log 'runs to 39 buckles ... across 19 summers, and two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work'; B recasts that as two thirds arriving soon after a tamping machine had been through, which is the passage's own agent for that work ('A tamping machine lifts the track and packs new stone underneath') and is what the record says and nothing more. The passage has already supplied the mechanism that makes the timing legible – jointed track left a winter gap for summer to close, whereas welded rail 'has nowhere to put the extra millimetres', so the force is held or not held by stone, and once the machine has packed fresh stone 'for eight weeks afterwards that stone is loose', the very window the tally counts – so a reader can both retrieve the detail and see why it is the interesting one. A = reversed order (reversed causality): it inverts the arrow, putting ballast work AFTER the buckle instead of before it, and it is tempting because the closing sentence does have gangs being sent wherever somebody has reported something. But that sentence is about which stretches enter the log at all – the point it makes is that 'the quieter miles go uncounted' – and it never says a reported buckle brings ballast work; the tally sentence fixes the order explicitly the other way round ('in the eight weeks after ballast work'). A second seam gives A away to a careful reader: the passage's agent for ballast work is the tamping machine, and gangs appear only in that reporting sentence, so a gang sent out 'to work the ballast' is an actor the text never puts on that job. C = quantifier_upgrade: 'two in three' absolutised to 'they all', with the passage's own eight-week window and its tamping machine kept in place so that the option reads like a faithful summary; C and the key now name the same agent, so the quantifier is the only thing that decides between them, which is exactly the reading the item is testing. A third of the logged buckles fell outside that window, which is precisely the proportion the passage is careful to state. D = outside_knowledge plus the intuition a reader brings to the topic – heat buckles rails, so the hottest weeks should hold the most buckles – and the log simply never says this. The passage's only direct evidence on the point cuts against D ('The hottest week on record produced none.'), though a single week is thin ground from which to refute a claim about weeks in the plural; the disqualifier that does the work is the tally itself, which is the log's own answer to when the buckles came – two in three of them in the eight weeks after ballast work – so D substitutes a clustering the record does not report. The twenty-seven-degree stress-free temperature is the passage's own warning against the intuition D trades on: the text says it tells Vessholm how hard a July afternoon will push against the rail and 'nothing about what is resisting it'. Hedge balance: the key is the specific, unhedged claim; the two hedged options ('usually' in A, 'most' in D) are both wrong and the single hard absolutiser ('all', in C) sits on a distractor, so neither 'pick the qualified answer' nor 'strip the absolutes' locates the key. Lengths under mech tokenization: key B 14 words against A 15 / C 14 / D 14, so the key is joint-shortest rather than longest (ratio 1.07, cap 2.36).

No -ize/-ise verbs are used, so no variety leak on that axis. The rationale field is generator-facing only.
generator_meta.originality_note: SEARCH LOG (all queries run 2026-08-25 via the Exa web-search MCP; the WebSearch tool's session budget was exhausted before name checking began, so no WebSearch queries were run). (1) Query "Isak Vessholm" OR "Esme Quillenby" person -> no bearer of either full name returned; top hits were unrelated individuals sharing only a given name (Isak Almgren, Uppsala; Isak Sebbas, Turku; Esme Tuttiett, London). (2) Query "Vessholm" -> no entity of that name surfaced; nearest returns were the real Swedish places Vaxholm (Stockholm County) and Vivesholm (Gotland), neither a person and neither the queried string. (3) Query "Quillenby" -> two hits only, neither a real person, firm or place: a suggested pet name on hedgehogcentral.com (2010) and OCR mangling of the mathematical term 'Barratt-Priddy-Quillen' on mathoverflow.net. (4) Distinctive-phrase probes of the passage's own wording were run against the same index (see phrase_probe_note). (5) Local topic screen: grep for ballast|buckle|welded rail|permanent way over data/parsed/*.json (28 sittings) returned no matches; the bare token 'rail' occurs 9 times in the authentic corpus, so there is no source-corpus passage on this topic. No real firm, network, standards body or publication is named anywhere in the unit; the district is deliberately left unnamed so that no toponym is invented. The 27-degree stress-free temperature and the tamping/lateral-resistance mechanism are generic permanent-way engineering, not a quotation of any body's standard; the 39-buckle tally, the 19 summers and the two-in-three finding are invented.
generator_meta.phrase_probe_note: Exact-phrase probes run 2026-08-25 via the Exa search MCP: "nowhere to put the extra millimetres" returned five results, none containing the phrase (all were renovation/tolerance essays about millimetre gaps); "the shoulder heaped beyond" returned five results, none containing the phrase (road-shoulder and unrelated literary texts). No published text carrying either wording surfaced. This is a two-phrase probe, not the full eight-phrase Tier-2 sweep specified in elf/anti-plagiarism.md, and no probe of the remaining sentences was run.
generator_meta.hedge_balance_note: Key B is the flat, specific claim. The two hedged options ('usually' in A, 'most' in D) are both wrong and the single hard absolutiser ('all', in C) sits on a distractor, so neither blind heuristic works. Under mech tokenization the options run A 15 / B 14 / C 14 / D 14: the key is joint-shortest, not longest, and the length ratio is 1.07, far under the 2.36 ELF cap.
generator_meta.residue_note: The fishplate opening, the twenty-seven-degree stress-free figure, the shoulder ballast beyond the sleeper ends and the closing worry about under-reported quiet miles are concrete residue the question never tests; the passage also ends by casting doubt on its own tally rather than resolving into a verdict, so it does not read as a ramp built toward its item.
generator_meta.clone_check_note: Move sequence deliberately unlike the shipped P5 ELF shorts: it opens on a historical contrast (jointed vs welded) rather than a negation ('A playground surface is not engineered to feel soft', elf-b9-004), a second-person scene ('Anyone who has stood in front of a paint display', elf-b12-003) or a premise statement ('A cabin window has to be a hole', elf-b13-003); it carries no direct quotation and no expert verdict; and it closes on the source's own doubt about the data instead of an aphoristic 'not A, but B' chiasmus (retired per law 12/15).
